processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Homogenization of the cast ingot before hot forging.
Hot forging performed in the temperature range 1050-800 °C.
Air cooling to room temperature after hot forging.

structures.overall_structure: Dual-phase microstructure of delta ferrite and austenite: austenite (mostly elongated) in a δ-ferrite matrix. XRD shows ferrite and austenite in the hot forged specimen; some remnant dendritic (cast) structure is still visible.

interfaces.phase_evolution: Austenite has not decomposed into a low-temperature transformation product (e.g. martensite) after hot forging; the ferrite present was formed during solidification as δ-ferrite and has not been consumed by austenite due to the high Al content. Austenite fraction is slightly (~3%) higher than in the cast specimen, attributed to elemental partitioning during soaking at high temperature.
interfaces.interface_notes: Remnant dendritic structure is still visible in the hot forged specimen (blue arrow, Fig. 2e), possibly due to insufficient soaking and dissolution before hot forging.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Bruker D8 advanced X-ray diffraction instrument equipped with Co-Kα (1.79 Å) target
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the major phases present in the developed steel after casting and hot forging
characterization_methods.key_findings: XRD shows presence of ferrite and austenite in both cast and hot forged specimens; the ferrite is presumed δ-ferrite based on the Thermo-Calc equilibrium phase fraction plot.
~29% (volume %) austenite in the forged sample (vs ~26% in cast).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Leica optical microscope; specimens etched with Villella's Reagent (5 ml HCl + 1 g picric acid + 100 ml ethanol) for 10-15 sec after colloidal polishing (0.25 µm)
characterization_methods.purpose: Confirm the dual-phase microstructure in cast and hot forged specimens
characterization_methods.key_findings: Confirms dual-phase microstructure in the hot forged specimen with elongated, aligned second phase; a remnant dendritic structure is arrowed (Fig. 2e).

characterization_methods.technique: Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscopy (FEG-SEM)
characterization_methods.purpose: Microstructural analysis of the hot forged specimen
characterization_methods.key_findings: SEM image (Fig. 2f) confirms individual phases of austenite (mostly elongated) in the δ-ferrite matrix.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: FEG-SEM (ZEISS VP 300) equipped with EBSD camera, operating at 20 kV, step size 0.5 µm; post-processing in TSL-OIM software
characterization_methods.purpose: Confirm the individual phases in the hot forged specimen
characterization_methods.key_findings: EBSD phase map superimposed on IQ map (Fig. 2g) shows elongated austenite islands (FCC, green) in the δ-ferrite (BCC, red) matrix in the forged sample.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS VP 300 SEM equipped with Energy Dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: At least 5-7 areas and 15-20 spots per phase; average reported with standard deviation
characterization_methods.key_findings: General method for elemental mapping/analysis of phases in the developed steel.

characterization_methods.technique: X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and Optical Emission Spectroscopy (OES)
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the final chemical composition of the developed steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: Measured composition (wt.%): Fe bal., Mn 7.79, Al 4.88, Si 0.84, C 0.2, P 0.03, S 0.03 (Table 1).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: BAHR DIL 850 dilatometer; cylindrical sample 4 mm diameter × 10 mm length prepared by wire EDM
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Heating rate 10 °C/s, holding temperature 1000 °C, holding time 5/15 minutes, cooling rate 1 °C/s
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine critical transformation temperatures of the hot forged specimen and correlate theoretical critical temperatures with actual ones
characterization_methods.key_findings: No significant deviation/hump in change in length during heating and cooling; only a slight deviation at ~600 °C (marked by black ellipse in Fig. 1c), indicating insignificant dissolution/transformation of ferritic phase. The two curves are labelled '5 min holding time' and '15 min holding time'.

characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the density of the developed steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: Density of 6.91455 g/cc; ~11.35% lower than conventional steel (~7.8 g/cc).

computational_details.simulation_method: CALPHAD thermodynamic equilibrium calculation (phase fraction vs temperature)
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Equilibrium calculation for the developed Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (wt.%) steel from liquid to room temperature
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Theoretical critical temperatures were correlated with the actual dilatometry curve measured on the forged sample; the duplex δ-ferrite + austenite region was predicted as ~650 °C to ~1350 °C and used to select the intercritical annealing temperature of 750 °C.

computational_details.simulation_method: Thermodynamic stacking fault energy (SFE) calculation using the Olson and Cohen model
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: Olson and Cohen thermodynamic model; values from literature [27-33]
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Assuming an initially finer austenite grain size of 40 µm; equilibrium austenite composition at 750 °C for Al, C, Mn and Si of 4.39%, 0.47%, 11.16% and 1.09% respectively
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Theoretical SFE of the designed steel ~35 mJ/m² falls in the 20-40 mJ/m² range. For the IA750_60 Min specimen, using EDS-measured reverted austenite Mn and Al (7.58±0.14 and 3.96±0.15), the SFE was calculated as ~27 mJ/m²; with C reduced to ~0.05 wt% the SFE falls to ~2 mJ/m².

analytical_models.equation_role: Computes stacking fault energy of austenite from Gibbs free energy change, molar surface density and interfacial surface energy
analytical_models.model_note: SFE calculated from molar Gibbs free energy changes (chemical, magnetic, excess), molar surface density (ρ = (4/√3)(1/a0²N)) and lattice parameter equation a0 = 3.5945 + 0.00125(%Mn-20) + 0.00594(%Al) + 0.0272(%C).

unmapped_findings: Hot forged specimen: the cast ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 hr and then hot forged to 50% thickness reduction in the temperature range 1050-800 °C, followed by air cooling to room temperature.

The hot forged specimen contains ~29 vol% austenite vs ~26 vol% in the cast specimen (Rietveld refinement of XRD) — a ~3% higher austenite fraction, attributed to some elemental partitioning during soaking at higher temperature that may increase the stability of the austenite phase.
A remnant dendritic structure is still visible in the hot forged specimen (blue arrow, Fig. 2e), possibly due to insufficient soaking and dissolution before hot forging.

Dilatometry performed on the hot-forged specimen (BAHR DIL 850; 4 mm dia × 10 mm cylinder; heating 10 °C/s; hold at 1000 °C for 5/15 min; cooling 1 °C/s) showed no significant deviation in the change in length apart from a slight deviation at ~600 °C; the two near-coincident traces were labelled '5 min holding time' and '15 min holding time'.

The δ-ferrite retained in the developed steel (including the hot forged state) is highly stable — its structure/morphology remains essentially unchanged after subsequent intercritical annealing; ~70 vol% δ-ferrite is present.
Nominal (designed) steel composition is Fe-8Mn-5Al-0.2C (wt.%); measured composition is Fe balance with Mn 7.79, Al 4.88, Si 0.84, C 0.2, P 0.03, S 0.03 wt.% (Table 1).
